body.p: questions then arise: “Who am I? What am I here for?” The social duties and tasks are no answer. It is necessary, but not enough, to find the way to one’s own solitary responsibility and freedom. The self is looking for a truth which it cannot reach by itself, but only in a communication with another self, a truth in which both are at the same time absolutely rooted, each in terms of its own human translation of Transcendence, and totally ready to recognize the translation of the other.

That means that neither can pretend to possess truth as such, no one is in possession of irrefutable arguments, to force the other to submission, as if it were possible for him to possess a direct and objective knowledge of Transcendence or a perfectly univocal Word of God. Here we see again: the non-possession of the transcendent truth, together with the certainty of Transcendence, is what makes true communication possible, as an endless search for meaning of the “inexhaustible ciphers”.

There is not only the failure to possess Transcendence in communication; communication itself is never completely realised. Each self is too narrow, or too possessive, or yields too easily to convenience. In communication, the two are not and should not be one. There is always guilt in this never ending and never won “loving fight”. But here the failure has once again a most precious result: thanks to this experience of failure, human beings deepen their sense for a truth which is beyond any particular knowledge, never possessed, and the condition for existential loving communication.

A last example: on the level of faith. For Jaspers there is more than a distinction, there is an opposition between the religious faith of somebody who belongs to a religious institution and recognizes the authority of certain persons or writings and what Jaspers calls “philosophical faith”. There is, as I have often observed, a constant misunderstanding about this question. The objections of Jaspers are by no means of an agnostic nature, they do not belong to the thinking of the “Aufklärung”. This can be shown with great evidence if we consider the discussion which took place between him and Bultmann, the protestant theologian. Paradoxically, the theologian recommended a modern “translation” of the Holy Scriptures, so as to make them acceptable for minds shaped by modern, scientific and objective thought, whereas the philosopher wanted to keep them in their literal authenticity. We must try to explain why: the reason is once again that it is necessary to go through a failure of the understanding if one wants to reach the transcendent meaning. It would be an error to change the religious language of the Holy Scriptures, which can be deciphered as a “Chiffreschrift” by a reader existentially engaged in front of Transcendence, to change it into a modern rationalised language giving the misleading illusion of an adequate, literal knowledge.
